notes.summary: Security's first principle: state your threat model. What is the attacker allowed to do — read packets? run code? control the admin? Nickolai Zeldovich's Fall 2014 recorded edition teaches security as explicit assumptions and mechanisms, with buffer overflow labs that make it hands-on. Every lecture here names its attacker before its defense.
notes.focus: Write the threat model for your Full Stack Ocean account system: who can do what, and which of those you defend against. Most real vulnerabilities are unstated models.

notes.summary: The classic exploit, dissected: unchecked input overflows a stack buffer, overwrites the return address, and hijacks control flow. The lab has you actually smash a stack in a contained environment — writing shellcode and jumping to it. Your 6.100L/6.004 stack-frame knowledge is the prerequisite that makes this concrete.
notes.focus: Draw the stack frame of the vulnerable function, marking where each input byte lands. The exploit is arithmetic once the diagram is right.

notes.summary: Defense in depth: ASLR, stack canaries, DEP/NX make raw exploitation harder; ROP chains adapt (lecture 3's continuation). The architectural answer is privilege separation — split programs so a compromised component controls little. OKWS-style designs treat every component as untrusted, which is how your own apps should think.
notes.focus: Take an app you've built (CS50 Finance counts) and split its components by privilege on paper: what breaks if each is compromised? That map IS the design.

notes.summary: Unforgeable tokens of authority: capabilities confine what code CAN do rather than vetting who it IS. File descriptors are capabilities; so are object references in capability languages. Sandboxing native code (lecture 7's topic) combines OS isolation with capability-style delegation — the browser's model for every extension and tab you use.
notes.focus: List three ambient-authority moments in your own code (reading env vars, implicit filesystem paths). Then sketch the capability version of each.

notes.summary: The browser's security architecture: same-origin policy as the load-bearing wall, DNS and certificates as naming, frames and postMessage for cross-origin communication. Every web app you've built (and this one) lives inside this model — understanding SOP's exact rules explains half of all web CVEs.
notes.focus: Compute SOP verdicts for 8 URL pairs, including tricky subdomains and ports. Precision here separates 'knows the web' from 'ships secure web apps'.

notes.summary: The web exploit family: XSS injects scripts into pages (stored, reflected, DOM-based), CSRF makes the browser act as the user, and SQL injection talks to your database. Defenses — output encoding, CSRF tokens, parameterized queries — are simple ONCE you can articulate the exact confusion each attack exploits.
concepts: The confusion pattern behind all three
notes.focus: Audit one of your own projects for all three bug classes with a checklist. Finding your first real XSS in your own code is this lecture's true assignment.

notes.summary: Program analysis for finding bugs: symbolic execution runs programs with symbolic inputs, collecting path constraints and solving them (SMT solvers) to reach deep code. Coverage-guided fuzzing (AFL-style) is its cheap cousin. These tools found thousands of real CVEs and are standard equipment in modern security engineering.
notes.focus: Write the path constraints for a simple check function, then hand-solve them to reach the error branch. You have just done a solver's job, at toy scale.

notes.summary: Attacking the network itself: TCP sequence prediction and off-path injection, BGP hijacking (your 6.829 knowledge returning as threat), and DNS spoofing. Defenses — TLS for confidentiality and authentication, and its CA trust roots — get the same assumption-based scrutiny. The lecture connects your networking course to its adversary.
notes.focus: Classify five attacks as on-path or off-path, then say which TLS property defeats each. The matrix organizes the whole lecture.

notes.summary: Protocols fail around cryptography, not inside it: replay attacks, downgrade negotiations, timing side channels, and re-ordering of unauthenticated fields. The lecture dissects real protocol flaws (the WEP/SSL family) with the message-flow diagrams your 6.829 training taught you to read. Nonce discipline and authenticate-everything emerge as the rules.
notes.focus: Draw one protocol's message flows and mark what is authenticated vs plaintext. Unauthenticated fields in a diagram = attack surface on a whiteboard.

notes.summary: The modern frontier: side channels leak secrets through timing, cache behavior, and power (Spectre/Meltdown changed the industry), and trusted hardware (SGX, TPMs) tries to enforce confidentiality even against the OS. These topics connect your 6.004 hardware instincts to the attacker's perspective.
notes.focus: Take the password-comparison loop and rewrite it constant-time. Then say WHY the naive version leaks length and prefix information.

notes.summary: What if the compiler enforced security? Type systems powerful enough to prevent SQL injection, XSS, and CSRF by construction — Ur/Web is the case study, where whole classes of web vulnerabilities are TYPE ERRORS. This lecture connects your CSE341 type theory to 6.858's attack classes: prevention by construction, not by vigilance.
notes.focus: Pick one attack class from the web lectures and sketch a type rule that would reject the vulnerable code. One rule, one dead vulnerability class.

notes.summary: Checkpoint across the exploit families: memory corruption, web attacks, network attacks, and the analysis tools. Your labs ARE the exam in this course — re-derive your buffer overflow exploit and your XSS findings from scratch. Security exams test exactly the attacker's reasoning loop.
notes.focus: Re-write your lab 1 exploit cold: stack diagram first, then input construction. Speed at THAT is the course's real certification.

practice.title: Final project: design a secure system

notes.summary: The synthesis: pick a system you know (this app qualifies!) and design its security end to end — assets, threat model, mechanisms, and residual risks, with the audit checklist from each unit applied. Security as a design discipline, not a checklist — that is 6.858's thesis, and your CS142 web apps next term inherit it.
notes.focus: Write Full Stack Ocean's security design doc: assets, attackers, mechanisms per unit, and open risks. A real system you actually use makes this final real.
